Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- The body of a fugitive U.S. marshal has been found in the city of Juarez, Mexico, according to the U.S. Marshals Service -- the latest discovery in a wave of violence that has gripped towns along the U.S.-Mexican border in recent months. The body of Deputy Marshal Vincent Bustamante was found Wednesday in Juarez, Mexico. The body of Deputy Marshal Vincent Bustamante -- who faced federal charges of stealing weapons and other government property -- was found in Juarez on Wednesday, said Marshals Service spokesman Jeff Carter. Bustamante appeared to have been shot in the back of the head, a federal law enforcement source said. Chihuahua state police said the body had multiple wounds to the head -- apparently consistent with an execution-style shooting, according to Edgar Roman, a reporter with XHIJ television in Juarez.  Watch where the U.S. Marshal's body was found » . Bustamante, 48, was charged with stealing U.S. government property including Glock and Ruger handguns, a shotgun and a pair of binoculars, according to court documents. According to the federal source, who was not authorized to speak about details of the case and asked not to be named, a pawnshop owner became suspicious when Bustamante attempted to pawn a shotgun and called the U.S. Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. The source said Bustamante would buy back items he had pawned on his pay days and return them. Bustamante's attorney, Mike Torres, said a warrant was issued for Bustamante's arrest after he failed to appear at a court hearing last week. He said Bustamante was a 17-year veteran of the marshals and a former El Paso Police officer who lived in El Paso with his wife and two children. "He was a familiar face around the federal courthouse here," Torres said. "I'm very shocked by this and very saddened. "He had a lot of friends and a lot of people that cared about him." Carter said Bustamante was on administrative leave from the marshals and had been required to turn in his gun and badge. He said Bustamante had not been in Mexico on marshals business and that all of the weapons he was charged with stealing had been recovered. Carter said Bustamante was on "modified status" with the marshals, meaning he had been required to turn in his gun and badge outside of his official work hours. "What I can tell you is that the U.S. Marshals Service is saddened by the death of Deputy Bustamante and our thoughts and prayers are with his family," he said. Carter said U.S. marshals are working with the FBI and Mexican authorities to investigate the death. He said an autopsy will be conducted in Mexico, and another may be conducted once Bustamante's body is returned to the United States. Juarez, which sits across the border from El Paso, Texas, has become one of the major battlegrounds as drug cartels fight both each other and Mexican authorities. The conflict has made violence increasingly common in Juarez, Tijuana and other Mexican border towns. More than 400 deaths in the region have been attributed to the fighting this year. CNN's Anderson Cooper, Emily Robards and Devon Sayers contributed to this report.

# Fugitive U.S. Marshal Found Shot to Death in Juárez as Cartel Violence Grips Border

**EL PASO, Texas —** A fugitive deputy U.S. marshal who disappeared while facing a federal criminal case was found dead across the border in Ciudad Juárez, Mexico, in what authorities described as an execution-style killing.

Vincent Bustamante, a veteran deputy assigned to the U.S. Marshals Service in El Paso, had been shot in the head, according to authorities investigating the death. His body was discovered in Juárez, placing the case in one of Mexico’s most violent drug-trafficking corridors at the height of a brutal struggle among rival cartels and security forces.

Mexican investigators were working to determine when and where Bustamante was killed and whether his death was connected to his legal troubles, his law-enforcement career or the wider criminal violence consuming the region. No clear motive was immediately established.

## Pawnshop transactions drew scrutiny

Before his disappearance, Bustamante had come under federal investigation involving government property and firearms. Court records and reports about the case indicated that pawnshop transactions helped lead investigators to items allegedly connected to him.

The activity raised particularly serious concerns because Bustamante was a federal law-enforcement officer with access to weapons and other official equipment. Authorities examined whether government property had been improperly removed, possessed or pawned.

The allegations remained unresolved at the time of his death. Bustamante had not completed the judicial process, and the case against him had not gone to trial.

## Missed court appearance preceded manhunt

Bustamante’s legal situation escalated when he failed to appear for a scheduled federal court hearing in El Paso. His absence prompted authorities to treat him as a fugitive and launch a search for one of their own.

The missed hearing also fueled questions about whether he had voluntarily crossed into Mexico, received help while evading arrest or been taken there against his will. Investigators did not immediately disclose evidence answering those questions.

His disappearance was unusual and embarrassing for the Marshals Service, an agency whose central responsibilities include tracking and arresting federal fugitives.

## Placed on administrative status

At the time the allegations surfaced, Bustamante had been removed from regular operational duties and placed on administrative status, according to officials. Such action can restrict an employee’s law-enforcement responsibilities while an internal or criminal investigation is pending, but it does not itself amount to a finding of guilt.

Officials emphasized that his employment status and the criminal allegations were separate from the investigation into his killing.

The U.S. Marshals Service said it was cooperating with other American agencies and Mexican authorities. Because the body was found in Mexico, the homicide investigation initially fell under Mexican jurisdiction, while U.S. investigators continued examining Bustamante’s flight and the federal case he had left behind.

## Killing occurred amid cartel bloodshed

Bustamante’s death came as Ciudad Juárez was experiencing extraordinary levels of violence tied to organized crime. The city, located directly across the Rio Grande from El Paso, had become a major battleground for control of smuggling routes used to move cocaine, marijuana and other drugs into the United States.

Rival trafficking organizations—including groups associated with the Juárez and Sinaloa cartels—fought for control of the lucrative corridor. Gunmen carried out assassinations in streets, homes, restaurants and vehicles, often using close-range shots and leaving victims’ bodies in public places.

Police officers, prosecutors, journalists, business owners and civilians were among those targeted. The scale of the killings strained local law enforcement and complicated efforts to distinguish cartel-related executions from personal disputes, robberies and other crimes.

The method used to kill Bustamante led to immediate speculation about organized crime, but authorities cautioned that an execution-style shooting does not, by itself, prove cartel involvement.

## Questions remain on both sides of the border

Investigators faced several central questions: why Bustamante entered Mexico, who knew he was in Juárez, whether the pawnshop and firearms allegations had any connection to his death, and whether his work as a deputy marshal made him a target.

They also sought to reconstruct his final movements after he missed court.

Bustamante’s death closed the search for a fugitive but opened a more complex cross-border homicide investigation—one involving a federal officer under indictment, disputed government property and a city where organized-crime killings had become grimly routine.

Authorities did not immediately announce arrests in the killing.
